title: Man. Post. Cap. II §XIX: Placeus — mediate looks to actual sin; reductio on Adam-habitus imputation; before Deinde habitus
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. First I did not say Adam's sin is imputed, inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. I only said that because hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, and a perverse propensity to such a sin, and so a habitual consent to that sin, I do not see a cause why it cannot be said to be imputed to us, namely that first sin which left the corruption called hereditary in Adam's soul. But that cannot be other than that first actual sin of Adam. For no other left that depravation in Adam's soul. You see, Reader, that I refer that imputation which I call mediate to Adam's actual sin, and give a reason why on account of that hereditary corruption it can be said to be imputed to us. But since the Learned Man proves that the corruption, inasmuch as it was in Adam's soul, is imputed to us, see please what follows. First that will be ours, as an actual sin, by imputation; for this is agreeable to his opinion. Does he therefore want Adam's posterity to be corrupt, as he speaks, interpretatively, or imputatively? Next I ask whether the corruption, inasmuch as it inheres in us, is imputed to us, or not? If you deny; then it is not truly sin, it does not make us guilty. If you say yes; then the corruption is imputed to us twice, once inasmuch as it was in Adam, again inasmuch as it is in us. So we are more guilty than Adam. Who would believe this? Finally I ask whether the corruption, inasmuch as it stuck in Adam, is imputed to us immediately, or by corruption mediating? If the latter, why is the same not said of the actual sin? If the former, Therefore our corruption is the punishment of that corruption of Adam: For why should the punishment of the imputed habitual not equally be, as of the imputed actual? If therefore it is the punishment of that imputed one, Adam's habitual sin is punished more in us than it was punished in Adam himself. For in us, if faith is had to the learned man, it is punished by the infliction of corruption, whereas that punishment was not Adam's corruption punished in Adam. Lastly, If the corruption as it was in Adam is imputed to us, either it is imputed to us together with his actual sin, or before, or after that sin. Why it should be imputed before or after that, a cause cannot be said. If it is imputed to us together, it was also imputed to Adam together with the actual—for why would those two sins of his not equally have been imputed together to him and to us? If therefore they were imputed together to Adam himself, his corruption was not the punishment of the actual sin: for it would have been prior to itself: for imputation precedes punishment; and it would have been imputed to Adam before it was in him. Which not obscurely implies a contradiction. But let him go on.
pass_b_english: Placeus: First, I never said Adam's sin is imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in his soul. My point was only this: hereditary corruption is that habit the first sin left there, plus a bent toward such sin, and so habitual consent to it—and I see no reason we may not say the first sin is imputed to us, namely the sin that left what we call hereditary corruption in Adam's soul. That can only be Adam's first actual sin; nothing else planted that depravity in him. So, Reader: the imputation I name mediate I refer to Adam's actual sin, and I explain why hereditary corruption lets us say it is imputed to us. But if the learned man proves the corruption as it stood in Adam's soul is imputed to us, watch what follows. First, that corruption becomes ours as an actual sin by imputation—his own view requires it. Does he then want Adam's posterity corrupt 'interpretatively' or 'imputatively'? Next: is the corruption as it inheres in us also imputed to us? Deny it, and it is not truly sin and does not make us guilty. Affirm it, and corruption is charged twice—once as it was in Adam, again as it is in us—so we are guiltier than Adam. Who believes that? Last: is Adam-stuck corruption imputed to us immediately, or through corruption as a means? If through a means, why not say the same of the actual sin? If immediately, then our corruption is the punishment of Adam's—for why should an imputed habitual not draw punishment as an imputed actual does? If so, Adam's habitual sin is punished harder in us than it was in him: in us, on his showing, by inflicted corruption, whereas that was not how Adam's own corruption was punished in Adam. Finally, if Adam's-as-was corruption is imputed to us, it comes with his actual sin, or before it, or after. Before or after has no cause. If together with us, it was together with Adam too—else why would those two sins not equally have hit him and us at once? If they hit Adam together, his corruption was not the punishment of the actual: it would be earlier than itself, since imputation precedes punishment, and it would be charged to him before it existed in him. That is open contradiction. But let him go on.
source_text: PLAC. Primum non dixi, imputari peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Tantum dixi, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa propensio ad ejusmodi peccatum, atque adeo consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, causam me non videre, cur non possit dici nobis imputari, nimirum primum illud peccatum, quod corruptionem, quae haereditaria vocatur, in Adami anima reliquit. Id autem aliud esse non potest quam primum illud Adae peccatum actuale. Aliud enim nullum illam deprauationem in Adami anima reliquit. Vides Lector, me imputationem illam, quam mediatam appello, referre ad peccatum Adae actuale, ac rationem reddere, cur ob haereditariam illam corruptionem dici possit nobis imputari. Sed quandoquidem Vir Doctus probat corruptionem, quatenus in Adami anima fuit, nobis imputari, vide quaeso quid consequatur. Primum illa nostra erit, ut peccatum actuale, per imputationem; hoc enim est illius sententiae consentaneum. Vultne igitur posteros Adami corruptos esse, ut loquitur, interpretative, seu imputative? Deinde, peto an corruptio, quatenus nobis inhaeret, nobis imputetur, necne? Si negas; igitur non est vere peccatum, non peragit nos reos. Si ais; igitur bis corruptio nobis imputatur, semel quatenus fuit in Adamo, iterum quatenus est in nobis. Ita magis rei sumus quam Adamus. Quis hoc credat? Denique peto an corruptio, quatenus haesit in Adamo, imputetur nobis immediate, an mediante corruptione? Si hoc, cur idem non dicitur de peccato actuali? Si illud, Ergo illius corruptionis Adae, nostra corruptio poena est: Cur enim non aeque imputati habitualis poena sit, ac imputati actualis? Si ergo illius imputati poena est, magis punitur in nobis peccatum habituale Adami, quam in ipso Adamo punitum est. In nobis enim, si viro Docto fides habetur, punitur inflictione corruptionis, cum ea poena non fuerit corruptio Adami in Adamo punita. Postremo, Si nobis imputatur corruptio ut fuit in Adamo, vel nobis imputatur simul cum eius peccato actuali, vel ante, aut post illud peccatum. Cur ante aut post illud imputetur, causa dici non potest. Si nobis simul imputatur, etiam simul cum actuali imputata fuit Adamo, cur non enim aeque simul illi ac nobis duo illa eius peccata imputata fuissent? Si ergo simul imputata fuerunt ipsi Adamo, eius corruptio non fuit poena peccati actualis: fuisset enim semetipsa prior: antecedit enim imputatio poenam; & prius imputata fuisset Adamo, quam in eo fuisset. Id quod non obscure contradictionem implicat. Sed pergat.
